mission: FHI was an Oxford research group founded by Nick Bostrom that brought philosophers, computer scientists, mathematicians and economists together to study humanity's long-term future. It helped create the ideas of existential risk, AI alignment, AI governance and longtermism. After a hiring and fundraising freeze from 2020, the university closed it in April 2024; its alumni now work across many successor organisations.

key_work.title: Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies (Nick Bostrom)
key_work.plain_summary: The book that brought AI existential risk to a mass audience: it argues a machine smarter than us could be impossible to control unless we solve the control problem first.

key_work.title: The Vulnerable World Hypothesis
key_work.plain_summary: Asks what happens if some future invention makes catastrophe easy for anyone; argues civilisation might then need much stronger global coordination and oversight.

key_work.title: The Unilateralist's Curse
key_work.plain_summary: Shows that when many people can each take a risky action alone, the most over-optimistic one tends to act — a reason for caution with dangerous information and technology.

key_work.title: Astronomical Waste
key_work.plain_summary: Argues that reducing the risk of extinction matters enormously because of how much future value is at stake — a founding argument for prioritising existential risk.

key_work.title: FHI technical reports archive (incl. Whole Brain Emulation roadmap, Racing to the Precipice, Comprehensive AI Services)
key_work.plain_summary: The preserved archive of FHI's technical reports, from brain emulation to models of AI races and Eric Drexler's 'AI as services' framing.

key_work.title: The Windfall Clause: Distributing the Benefits of AI for the Common Good
key_work.plain_summary: Proposes that AI firms pledge in advance to share extreme profits widely if they ever earn a huge share of world output — work from FHI's governance team, now GovAI.

warnings.text: Humanity faces existential risks — events that could end or permanently cripple our future — and these are badly neglected.
A superintelligent AI whose goals differ from ours could be impossible to control after the fact.
Some technologies may make catastrophe easy to cause (the 'vulnerable world' worry).
Racing dynamics between AI developers can push them to cut corners on safety.

recommendations.text: Treat reducing existential risk as a top global priority.
Solve the AI control problem before building superintelligence.
Build global coordination and governance capacity for dangerous technologies.
Take care with hazardous information (information hazards) and avoid unilateral risky actions.
